Case 1
access set, and the child page table still has valid entries: the ager must descend, and the access bit cannot be cleared.

div.div:
Case 2
access set, but the child page table has no valid or transition entries: clear the access bit. The count of those entries is stored in the PFN.

div.div: All these zero PTEs get immediately skipped once the valid bit is zero. Therefore, the child tables and their child tables aren't looked at. In a single-level world I would have to scan 16 PTEs to see that they are all invalid, whereas I can skip them all with one check.

div.div:
User walk — slicing the virtual address
A virtual address is not searched for, it is sliced. Each layer takes a fixed field of bits from the address and uses it directly as an index into that layer's page table. If the PTE that is indexed into is invalid, the user takes a page fault and fills the PTE accordingly.
The lowest bits are never used to index anything — they are the offset into the page itself.
This address slices into (1, 3, 1, offset): entry 1 of the root, entry 3 of the interior table, entry 1 of the leaf, and then the offset picks the byte inside the data page.
Drawn with 4 entries per table, so 2 bits per layer. The real tree uses 9 bits per layer to index 512 entries, and a 12-bit offset.
